**NOTE 1:** This RMarkdown file reproduces all of the pre-registered analyses along with several exploratory analyses. Exploratory analyses of differential attrition are not directly reproducible as that would require use of "raw" datasets that have not been made publicly available. Please contact Calvin Lai (calvinlai@wustl.edu) if you would like access to those analyses.

**NOTE 2:** This file was adapted for public use and may contain errors. If you notice any statistical errors, missing info, or are just having trouble understanding the analyses, feel free to contact Calvin Lai (calvinlai@wustl.edu).

**NOTE 3:** To aid reading, I have written this report by adapting Sections 2, 3, 5, 6, and 9 from the Pre-Registration.

**NOTE 4:** To get this to run, you'll need to change "C:/Users/cklai/Dropbox/Projects/18_mib/scripts/osf/data/" to your personal directory.


2)  **Hypothesis.** What's the main question being asked or hypothesis being tested in this study?

*Question 1*: Does the Managing Implicit Bias (MIB) training program change police officers' [knowledge] of bias, concern about bias, motivation to address bias, intentions to use strategies to manage the impact of bias, and self-reported use of strategies to manage the impact of bias?

*Question 2:* How does the efficacy of the program change based on characteristics of the participant?

*Question 3*: How does the efficacy of the program change based on characteristics of the session?

3)  **Dependent variable.** Describe the key dependent variable(s) specifying how they will be measured.

KNOWLEDGE OF BIAS: We will take the average of three Likert-style questions ("Subtle or implicit biases influence my decision making about other people.", "Whether I am aware of it or not, I use a person's race or ethnicity to form an impression of the kind of person they are.", "My cultural background influences how I perceive other people.").

PERCEIVED MALLEABILITY OF BIAS: We will take the average of two Likert-style questions ("People have a certain amount of bias toward other people and they can't really change that.", "People's level of bias toward other people is something very basic about them that they can't change very much.").

CONCERN ABOUT BIAS: Participants are asked six questions assessing agreement/disagreement to the statement, "I worry that I act in an unintentionally biased way toward [White/Black/Asian/Hispanic or Latino/Gay, Lesbian, or Bisexual/Transgender] people." The question about White people was only in Time 1 and Time 2 and will not be used for analysis.
We will analyze the data as the average of the five other questions.

INTENDED STRATEGY USE (Time 2 only): For analysis, we will take the average of 5 questions assessing plans to use strategies.

ACTUAL STRATEGY USE (Time 1 and Time 3 only): For analysis, will take the average of 5 questions assessing actual use of strategies.

# Creating cohen d round function
cohensd <- function(pre, post){
  round((mean(post, na.rm=T)-mean(pre, na.rm=T)) / sd(post-pre, na.rm=T),2)
}

### General approach to reporting and interpreting findings
I conducted the analyses with data from participants that contributed to all time points (N = 53) alongisde other subsamples of the data which had larger sample sizes: T1+T2 (N = 347), T1+T3 (N = 173), T2+T3 (N = 74). I did not do cross-sectional analyses of individual time points which includes unmatched data (Ns = 2883, 620, 300) due to concerns about data fidelity.

I tried to interpret the data holistically by examining consistencies across different analyses, with greater weight given to larger subsamples of the data. 

For Question 1 (overall effect of training), I ran analyses with all relevant time points. For Questions 2 and 3 (Moderation by Participant and Session Characteristics), I focused just on all three timepoints (N = 53) and T1-T2 (N = 347). This was done to keep things manageable, but would definitely be open to arguments for being more exhaustive.

For all analyses, Time was operationalized as a categorical variable.

# Correlation Matrices
# Function to compute p-values of correlations
# mat : is a matrix of data
# ... : further arguments to pass to the native R cor.test function
cor.mtest <- function(mat, ...) {
    mat <- as.matrix(mat)
    n <- ncol(mat)
    p.mat<- matrix(NA, n, n)
    diag(p.mat) <- 0
    for (i in 1:(n - 1)) {
        for (j in (i + 1):n) {
            tmp <- cor.test(mat[, i], mat[, j], ...)
            p.mat[i, j] <- p.mat[j, i] <- tmp$p.value
        }
    }
  colnames(p.mat) <- rownames(p.mat) <- colnames(mat)
  p.mat
}

# Function to compute df of correlations
# mat : is a matrix of data
# ... : further arguments to pass to the native R cor.test function
cor.dftest <- function(mat, ...) {
    mat <- as.matrix(mat)
    n <- ncol(mat)
    p.mat<- matrix(NA, n, n)
    diag(p.mat) <- 0
    for (i in 1:(n - 1)) {
        for (j in (i + 1):n) {
            tmp <- cor.test(mat[, i], mat[, j], ...)
            p.mat[i, j] <- p.mat[j, i] <- tmp$parameter
        }
    }
  colnames(p.mat) <- rownames(p.mat) <- colnames(mat)
  p.mat
}

### Primary Analyses: Question 1
*Question 1*: To understand whether the training changed our key outcomes, we will conducted mixed models using the following equation: Key Outcome=Time+(1 \|Subject)

**General Summary**: 

- Officers showed a moderate to large increase in knowledge of bias immediatelyn after training (d = `r cohensd(t1t2$knowledge.t1, t1t2$knowledge.t2)`) that persisted a month later. 
- Officers perceived bias to be less malleable immediately after training (d = -.27), but they returned to baseline levels a month later (d = .38).
- Officers were more concerned about bias immediately after training (d = .36), but they returned to baseline levels a month later (d = -.27).
- Officers perceived understanding of the strategies remained stable a month after the training, but perceived efficacy and motivation to use strategies declined.
- Officers showed large increases in intentions to use strategies to mitigate bias (relative to actual strategy use) immediately after training. However, officers  reported *less* strategy use at Time 3 than Time 1. This may be due to a contrast effect; officers may have gained a more narrow sense of how to use these strategies effectively, and may have realized that they failed to live up to their intentions. Or, they may have tried to intentionally use the strategies to mitigate bias and felt that they were impractical.

\

#### Knowledge
**Summary**: Officers showed a moderate-large increase in knowledge of bias from baseline to Time 2 (d = 
`r cohensd(t1t2$knowledge.t1, t1t2$knowledge.t2)`). This increase in knowledge seemed to remain stable through Time 3 (d = 
`r cohensd(t2t3$knowledge.t2, t2t3$knowledge.t3)`). Time 3 remained substantially higher than Time 1 (d = This increase in knowledge seemed to remain stable through Time 3 (d = `r cohensd(t1t3$knowledge.t1, t1t3$knowledge.t3)`).

\

#### Perceived Malleability of Bias
**Summary**: Officers showed a small decrease in perceived malleability of bias from baseline to Time 2 (d = `r cohensd(t1t2$theories.t1, t1t2$theories.t2)`). However, perceived malleability of bias dropped in Time 3 relative to Time 2  (d = `r cohensd(t2t3$theories.t2, t2t3$theories.t3)`).It returned to baseline levels (d = `r cohensd(t1t3$theories.t1, t1t3$theories.t3)`).


##### All time points (total N = 53)
`r knitr::kable(summary(lmer(theories ~ time + (1|id), data = allLong))$coefficients, digits = c(2, 2, 2, 2, 3))`

##### Time 1 to Time 2 (total N = 347)
`r knitr::kable(summary(lmer(theories ~ time + (1|id), data = t1t2Long))$coefficients, digits = c(2, 2, 2, 2, 3))`

##### Time 1 to Time 3 (total N = 173)

#### Concern about Bias
**Summary**: Officers showed a small-moderate increase in concern about bias from baseline to Time 2 (d = `r cohensd(t1t2$biasworry.t1, t1t2$biasworry.t2)`). However, concern about bias dropped in Time 3 relative to Time 2 (d = `r cohensd(t2t3$biasworry.t2, t2t3$biasworry.t3)`). It returned to baseline levels (d = `r cohensd(t1t3$biasworry.t1, t1t3$biasworry.t3)`).

#### Strategy Use / Intentions
**Summary**: Officers showed intentions to use strategies to mitigate bias above baseline levels at Time 2 (d = `r cohensd(t1t2$strategy_use, t1t2$strategy_intend)`). However, participants at Time 3 unexpectedly reported less strategy use than at Time 1 (d = `r cohensd(t1t3$strategy_use, t1t3$strategy_used)`). This may be due to a contrast effect; officers may have gained a more narrow sense of how to use these strategies effectively, and may have realized that they failed to live up to their intentions. Or, they may have tried to intentionally use the strategies to mitigate bias and felt that they were impractical (see findings on perceived efficacy / motivation).

Officers are also reported less use of strategies relative to Time 2 intentions `r cohensd(t2t3$strategy_intend, t2t3$strategy_used)`).

### Primary Analyses: Question 2
*Question 2:* To understand how program efficacy depends on characteristics of the participant, we will conduct mixed models using the following equation:

Key Outcome=Time+SubjectCharacteristic+Time*SubjectCharacteristic+ (1 \|Subject)\
*We will assess the following subject characteristics (operationalization in parentheses):\
- Perceptions of respect from citizens (continuous)\
- Centrality of law enforcement identity (continuous)\
- Contact with minority group members (continuous)\
- Years in department (continuous)\
- Rank (Sergeant or above vs. Below Sergeant)\
- Race or ethnicity (White vs. Non-White; Black vs. Non-Black)\
- Gender (Male vs. Female)\
- Level of education (Bachelor's Degree or above vs. No Bachelor's Degree)\
- Perceived feasibility, efficacy, and motivation to use strategies (for intended & actual strategy use only) (continuous)\
- [Knowledge of] bias, perceived malleability of bias, concern about bias (for all key outcomes except themselves) (continuous)\
\

**General Summary**: 

- None of the demographic characteristics, past experiences, or general individual differences consistently moderated training effects.
- Perceptions of the strategies themselves did not moderate intended or actual strategy use either.
- The only consistent moderators were baseline knowledge of bias, perceived malleability of bias, and concern about bias.
- Moderator analyses with baseline knowledge of bias indicate  a "leveling" between people who were less knowledgeable and more knowledge about bias at baseline. That would suggest the training is more effective for officers who knew less about bias to begin with.
- Officers who perceived bias to be more malleable at baseline showed larger gains in knowledge, concerns about bias, and intentions to use strategies to mitigate bias at Time 2. However, these effects did not seem to persist through Time 3.
- Officers who were more concerned about bias at baseline showed smaller increases in knowledge of bias at Time 2, which may bias may be attributable to higher baseline knowledge of bias at Time 1 (i.e., a "leveling" effect similar to the knowledge moderator findings). Officers who were more concerned about bias at baseline also showed larger increases in the perceived malleability of bias at Time 2, which may reflect learning about strategies to mitigate bias.
\

#### Knowledge of bias (for all key outcomes except themselves) (continuous)
**Summary**: Officers with greater baseline knowledge of bias showed less of a decrease in perceived malleability of bias at Time 2, which may be attributable to lower perceived malleability in bias to begin with. Officers with greater baseline knowledge also showed smaller gains in concerns about bias, which may also be attributable to greater baseline concerns. Overall, these findings indicate  a "leveling" between people who were less knowledgeable and more knowledge about bias at baseline. That would suggest the training is more effective for officers who knew less about bias to begin with.

### Primary Analyses: Question 3
*Question 3*: To understand how program efficacy depends on characteristics of the sessions, we will conduct mixed models using the following equation:\
Key *Outcome=Time+SessionCharacteristic+Time*SessionCharacteristic+ (1\|Subject)\
We will assess the following subject characteristics (operationalization in parentheses):\
- Number of attendees (continuous)\
- Facilitator pair gender (male-male, male-female, female-female)\
- Facilitator pair race (Black-White, White-White, or Asian-Black/White)\
- Whether the facilitator pair contained an ex-member of law enforcement (Yes vs. No)\
- Whether the facilitator pair contained someone who had a connection to law enforcement (Yes vs. No; Yes vs. No (excluding ex-members of
law enforcement)).

**General summary**: Characteristics of the session generally did not matter.


\

#### Descriptive statistics & correlations by subject & session characteristics

We compared descriptive statistics and correlations by subject characteristics and session-level characteristics.
[NOTE: For brevity, these analyses were  not included in this report. Descriptive statistics and correlations were used to complement and assist with the interpretation of the primary inferential tests].


\

### Exploratory  Analyses

\

#### Differential attrition

**Summary**: I found considerable evidence of differential attrition. To examine differential attrition, I conducted 48 t-tests comparing 16 baseline variables in each of three merged subsamples (T1+T2, T1+T3, and all time points) against the portion of the T1 subsample that was not in the merged subsamples (hereafter, "no-show Time 1 sample"). In total, 18 of the 48 tests yielded significant differences.  Here's what I found:

*Contact Experiences*: The most consistent difference from the no-show Time 1 subsample was contact with Black and Hispanic people. Officers in the no-show Time 1 subsamples had less contact with Black individuals (Ms = 4, 4.02, 4.03) than T1+T2 (M = 4.3, d = 0.25, p < .001), T1+T3 (M = 4.31, d = 0.24, p < .001), and all time points (M = 4.3, d = 0.22, p = .0042). Officers in the no-show Time 1 subsamples had similarly less contact with Hispanic individuals (M = 3.62, 3.64, 3.65) than T1+T2 (M = 3.93, d = 0.21, p < .001), T1+T3 (M = 3.91, d = 0.2, p < .001), and all time points (M = 4.02, d = 0.28, p < .001).

*Officer rank*: Officers who participated in Time 3 (i.e., the T1+T3 or all time points subsamples) tended to be more senior and more highly ranked than the no-show Time 1 subsample.

- Years Worked (No-show Time 1 subsample vs. T1+T3): Ms = 15.83 vs. 17.71, d = 0.17, p = .012.
- Years Worked (No-show Time 1 subsample vs. all time points): Ms = 15.9 vs. 18.34, d = 0.22, p = .066.
- Rank (No-show Time 1 subsample vs. T1+T3): Ms = 15% vs.27% Sergeant or above, d = 0.34, p = .0010.
- Rank (No-show Time 1 subsample vs. all time points): Ms = 15% vs. 32% Sergeant or above, d = 0.47, p = .015.

*Other Characteristics that did not reliably replicate*: I also found a couple baseline differences that did not replicate consistently across subsample contrasts. Here they are:

- Officers who participated in T1 + T2 expected more respect from citizens (Ms = 4.47 vs. 4.81, d = 0.22, p < .001) and saw being a police officer as more identity-central (Ms = 3.89 vs. 4.20, d = 0.2, p < .001). They were also less concerned about bias (Ms = 2.24 vs. 2.07, d = -.11, p = .035).

- Officers who participated in T1 + T3 used more of the strategies to mitigate bias at baseline (Ms = 1.85 vs. 2.16, d = 0.16, p = .018).

- Officers who participated in all three time points were more likely to be more likely to be White (37% vs. 54%, d = .36, p = .026) and had less contact with LGB people (d = -.31, p = .020) and trans people (d = -.25, p = .035).


\

#### Mixed models with random slopes
Pre-registration: "We may re-estimate some of the mixed models described above with random slopes of time for participants."
\

**Summary**: I abandoned this approach due to convergence issues. Fitting time as a numeric variable rather than a categorical variable helped make some of the the models run, but was theoretically ill-fitting (Time 3 was expected to drop after Time 2) and generally explained little variance. I also tried  a random slope of training date (i.e., what session they took), but that also led to convergence issues or explained little variance.


\
